Label: Social security agreements: the states and what they coordinate
Description: The states outside the EU and EFTA with which Switzerland has a social security agreement, and what such an agreement coordinates in the AHV and IV.
Aliases: social security agreement countries; which countries have a social security agreement with Switzerland; totalization agreement; Sozialversicherungsabkommen Staaten; Abkommen soziale Sicherheit Liste; Sozialversicherungsabkommen; bilaterale Abkommen; Entsendeabkommen; Beitragsrückerstattung; Soziale Sicherheit; Vertragsstaaten; Mindestbeitragsdauer
Questions: Which countries have a social security agreement with Switzerland?; Hat die Schweiz mit meinem Heimatland ein Sozialversicherungsabkommen?
Published facts:
The Central Compensation Office addresses nationals of the following states with a social security agreement who do not live in Switzerland: Albania, Australia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Brazil, Chile, Israel, Japan, Canada, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Kosovo, the Philippines, Quebec, San Marino, Serbia, Tunisia, Türkiye, the USA, Uruguay and the United Kingdom.
Switzerland concluded bilateral agreements to coordinate parts of its social insurance system, in particular the AHV and the IV, with states outside the EU and EFTA. Most of them cover several branches and contain coordination rules for benefits; a minority, the posting agreements, contain only rules on posting workers to the other contracting state and on the refund of contributions.
The bilateral agreements apply to nationals of both contracting states who are or were subject to the social security law of one of them, and to their family members and survivors. Nationals of third states are sometimes included, as are refugees and stateless persons with their family members.
Every bilateral agreement covers old age, death (survivors' benefits) and invalidity. Some also cover sickness, accidents at work and family allowances under the federal rules for agriculture.
The main effects in the AHV and IV are equal treatment of the other state's nationals, a single applicable social security law (as a rule the law of the state where the person works, with posting as the exception), and the export of ordinary AHV and IV pensions worldwide where the agreement provides for it. Ordinary IV pensions below 50 per cent are limited to Swiss territory, and some agreements provide for a lump-sum settlement, a refund of AHV contributions or their transfer to a foreign social insurance.
A claim for benefits is filed with the social insurance institution of the contracting state of the place of stay; an AHV or IV pension claim filed with the foreign institution is forwarded by it to the Swiss Compensation Office or to the IV office for insured persons abroad.
Each state sets its own conditions and calculation. In Switzerland an ordinary old-age and survivors' pension requires a minimum contribution period of one year, and an ordinary invalidity pension a minimum contribution period of three years.

Label: Refund of AHV contributions on leaving Switzerland
Description: Who can have AHV contributions refunded after leaving Switzerland for good, by nationality group, and the general conditions of a refund (ZAS, RV-AHV).
Aliases: OASI contributions refund; OASI; erste Säule zurück; Rentenversicherung Beiträge zurück; AHV refund; refund of AHV contributions; get my AHV contributions paid back; AHV contributions back; AHV contributions refund leaving Switzerland; moving back home AHV; first pillar refund; AHV-Beiträge zurück; AHV-Beiträge zurückfordern; AHV Rückerstattung; Beiträge zurückbezahlt; AHV Rückvergütung Wegzug; Rückvergütung; Sozialversicherungsabkommen; Staatsangehörigkeit; EU/EFTA; mindestens ein Jahr Beiträge; endgültig; Rentenanspruch; Rückerstattung ihrer Beiträge; Rückvergütungsbetrag
Questions: I'm a German citizen moving back to Berlin for good after six years in Zurich. Can I get my AHV contributions paid back?; Kann ich meine AHV-Beiträge zurückfordern, wenn ich die Schweiz endgültig verlasse?
Published facts:
ZAS publishes a refund of AHV contributions for nationals of a state with which Switzerland has concluded no social security agreement.
ZAS publishes a refund of AHV contributions, under certain conditions, for nationals of Australia, Brazil, China, India, the Philippines, South Korea, Tunisia and Uruguay.
ZAS states that nationals of Switzerland and of an EU/EFTA state have no entitlement to a refund of their AHV contributions; it publishes a refund for nationals of a state without a social security agreement with Switzerland and, under certain conditions, for nationals of Australia, Brazil, China, India, the Philippines, South Korea, Tunisia and Uruguay.
ZAS states that nationals of a state whose social security agreement with Switzerland does not provide for the refund of contributions have no entitlement to a refund.
ZAS states that nationals of Australia, Brazil, Tunisia, Uruguay and the Philippines have the choice between the payment of a pension and the refund of their contributions.
To apply for a refund, the person must have paid AHV contributions for at least one year.
For a refund, the person and their family (spouse and children under 25) must have left Switzerland or firmly intend to leave it for good; adult children under 25 who stay in Switzerland must have completed their education.
ZAS pays the refund once the person has settled abroad for good.
RV-AHV Article 1: foreign nationals whose home state has no agreement with Switzerland, and their survivors, can reclaim the AHV contributions if these were paid for at least one full year in total and give rise to no pension entitlement; the nationality at the time of the claim counts.
ZAS states that a national of a state without a social security agreement who receives an AHV pension and moves abroad is in principle entitled to a refund of the contributions, from which the pensions already received are deducted.

Label: AHV pensions and benefits after moving abroad
Description: Whether an AHV pension, a helplessness allowance or supplementary benefits continue after moving abroad, by nationality group (ZAS).
Aliases: AHV pension abroad; AHV pension paid abroad; keep my AHV pension after moving abroad; what happens to my AHV contributions; pension after leaving Switzerland; AHV-Rente im Ausland; AHV-Rente Wegzug; Rente ins Ausland; AHV-Rente; Sozialversicherungsabkommen; Hilflosenentschädigung; Ergänzungsleistung; Ausgleichskasse; Zahlungsadresse; Hinterbliebenenrente; Israelische Staatsangehörige
Questions: I receive an AHV pension and move abroad. Do I keep it?; What happens to my AHV contributions if I cannot get them refunded?; Bekomme ich meine AHV-Rente weiter, wenn ich die Schweiz verlasse?
Published facts:
ZAS: a recipient of an AHV pension who is a national of a state without a social security agreement with Switzerland loses the pension on moving abroad.
ZAS: Swiss nationals, nationals of an EU or EFTA state and nationals of a state with a social security agreement with Switzerland keep their AHV pension when they move abroad.
ZAS: they must announce their departure to the compensation office that has paid the benefit, which passes the pension file to the Swiss Compensation Office SAK in Geneva; SAK then pays the pension to a payment address in Switzerland or abroad chosen by the recipient.
ZAS: Israeli nationals are entitled to a pension only if they also live in Israel or Switzerland.
ZAS: a recipient of a survivors' pension who is a national of a state without an agreement keeps the benefit abroad if the deceased person was Swiss or a national of a state with a social security agreement.
ZAS: a helplessness allowance and supplementary benefits to the AHV or IV (Ergänzungsleistungen) are granted only to persons living in Switzerland and are lost on settling abroad.

Label: Cash payment of pension fund assets on leaving Switzerland
Description: When occupational pension (BVG) assets can be paid out in cash on leaving Switzerland for good, the restriction for moves to the EU, Iceland, Norway and Liechtenstein, and the spouse's consent (BSV, FZG).
Aliases: zweite Säule auszahlen; Betriebsrente auszahlen; pension fund cash out; pension fund payout leaving Switzerland; whole pension fund paid out in cash; cash payment pension fund; second pillar withdrawal moving abroad; vested benefits moving abroad; Pensionskasse auszahlen; Pensionskassenguthaben bar beziehen; Pensionskasse Auswanderung; Freizügigkeitsguthaben auszahlen; 2. Säule Auszahlung Wegzug; Barauszahlung; BVG-Altersguthabens; überobligatorischen Teils; Vorsorgekapitals; Austrittsleistung; Vorsorgeeinrichtung; Auffangeinrichtung; schriftliche Zustimmung; Freizügigkeitsleistung; endgültig
Questions: I'm moving from Zurich to Munich for good and start a job there. Can I have my whole pension fund paid out in cash?; Kann ich mein Pensionskassenguthaben bar beziehen, wenn ich die Schweiz endgültig verlasse?
Published facts:
BSV: a cash payment of the BVG retirement assets is possible when the insured person proves that they are leaving Switzerland for good to settle abroad.
BSV: for married insured persons, the cash payment requires the written consent of the spouse.
BSV: since 1 June 2007, a cash payment of the BVG pension assets is no longer possible on moving to an EU state, Iceland or Norway if the person remains insured there against the risks of old age, death and disability.
BSV: the extra-mandatory part of the pension capital (as opposed to the BVG minimum) can still be paid out in that case.
BSV: on leaving Switzerland for good for Liechtenstein, a cash payment is excluded.
BSV: since 1 November 2021 national law applies to the United Kingdom, so persons who move to the United Kingdom can request the cash payment of their whole vested benefit, mandatory and extra-mandatory.
FZG Article 25f: insured persons cannot request a cash payment of the retirement assets under Article 15 BVG acquired up to leaving the pension fund if they remain compulsorily insured against old age, death and disability under the law of an EU member state, Iceland or Norway, or if they live in Liechtenstein.
FZG Article 5: insured persons can request the cash payment of the vested benefit when they leave Switzerland for good, subject to Article 25f; for married persons or registered partners it is permitted only with the written consent of the spouse or partner.
FZG Article 4: insured persons who do not join a new pension fund must tell their pension fund in which permitted form they want to keep their pension cover; without that notice, the pension fund transfers the vested benefit with interest to the substitute occupational benefit institution (Auffangeinrichtung) at the earliest six months and at the latest two years after the vesting event.

Label: FZA: coordination of social security
Description: What the treaty's coordination of social security systems ensures: equal treatment, the applicable law, aggregation of insurance periods and payment of benefits across borders (FZA Art. 8).
Aliases: social security coordination EU Switzerland; insurance periods EU countries count; Koordinierung der Sozialversicherung; Versicherungszeiten zusammenrechnen; Koordinierung der Systeme der sozialen Sicherheit; Versicherungszeiten; Zahlung der Leistungen
Questions: Do my pension contributions in an EU country count in Switzerland?; Werden meine Versicherungszeiten aus einem EU-Staat angerechnet?
Published facts:
FZA Article 8: the contracting parties coordinate their social security systems under Annex II to ensure in particular equal treatment; the determination of the applicable legislation; the aggregation of all insurance periods counted under the various national laws for acquiring and keeping entitlement to benefits and for calculating them; the payment of benefits to persons resident in the territory of the contracting parties; and mutual administrative assistance and cooperation.

Label: Tax at source: federal rules
Description: Who is taxed at source in Switzerland, the federal threshold of CHF 120,000 for the subsequent ordinary assessment and the 31 March request deadline (ESTV, QStV).
Aliases: Lohnsteuer; Lohnsteuerabzug; Steuerabzug vom Lohn; tax at source; taxed at source; withholding tax on salary; source tax; tax return tax at source; Quellensteuer; an der Quelle besteuert; Quellensteuer Schweiz; Quellensteuer zahlen; which canton's tax-at-source rules apply; Quellensteuer welcher Kanton; Niederlassungsbewilligung; Grenzgängerinnen; Quellensteuerpflicht; nachträglich ordentlich veranlagt; Zweiverdienerehepaare; Bruttoeinkommen; Steuerverwaltung; Säule 3a; Verwirkungsfrist
Questions: Who is taxed at source in Switzerland?; Werde ich mit einer B-Bewilligung an der Quelle besteuert?
Published facts:
ESTV: tax at source is deducted directly from the income of employees with tax residence in Switzerland who do not hold a settlement permit (C permit), and of employees without tax residence in Switzerland, for example cross-border commuters.
ESTV: employers deduct the tax at source from the salary of the employees concerned and transfer it to the competent cantonal tax administration.
ESTV: the tax-at-source tariff depends on the canton and can be obtained from the cantonal tax administrations.
QStV Article 9(1): a person is subsequently assessed in the ordinary procedure if their gross income from employment reaches at least CHF 120,000 in a tax year.
QStV Article 9(3): double-earner married couples are subsequently assessed in the ordinary procedure if the gross income of the husband or the wife reaches at least CHF 120,000 in a tax year.
QStV Article 9(4): the subsequent ordinary assessment is kept until the tax-at-source liability ends, even if the gross income falls temporarily or permanently below CHF 120,000 or the spouses divorce or separate.
ESTV: a person living in Switzerland and taxed at source who wants to deduct pillar 3a contributions must request a subsequent ordinary assessment from the tax administration of the canton of residence by 31 March of the year following the due date of the taxable payment; the deadline is a forfeiture deadline that cannot be extended, a late request is not considered, and in the following years until the liability ends the forms are sent automatically.

Label: Tax at source in the Canton of Zurich: liability and its end
Description: Who is liable to tax at source in the Canton of Zurich, and the end of the liability with the C permit, Swiss citizenship or marriage to a person holding either (Kantonales Steueramt, ZStB 87.3).
Aliases: tax at source Zurich; still taxed at source; marry a Swiss citizen tax at source; end of tax at source; B permit tax at source Zurich; Quellensteuer; Quellensteuer Zürich; heiraten; Schweizer heiraten; Heirat Quellensteuer; weiterhin an der Quelle besteuert; C-Bewilligung Quellensteuer; quellensteuerpflichtig; Niederlassungsbewilligung C; ordentliche Veranlagung; Schweizer Bürgerrecht; Quellensteuerpflicht; Folgemonat; Steuererklärung; Steuerschlussrechnung; eingetragener Partnerschaft; Schweizer Pass
Questions: Ich habe eine B-Bewilligung, arbeite in Zürich und heirate nächsten Monat einen Schweizer. Werde ich weiterhin an der Quelle besteuert?; I have a B permit, work in Zurich and marry a Swiss citizen next month. Will I still be taxed at source?
Published facts:
Canton of Zurich: a person resident in the canton is liable to tax at source if they hold neither the settlement permit C nor Swiss citizenship, work for an employer based in Switzerland, and are not married to or in a registered partnership with a person who holds the C permit or Swiss citizenship.
Canton of Zurich: employers based in Switzerland deduct the tax at source from the salary automatically, so employees must tell their employer that they are liable to tax at source.
Canton of Zurich: for persons resident in Switzerland, the tax-at-source liability ends when they receive the settlement permit C or a Swiss passport, marry a person with the C permit or a Swiss passport who lives in Switzerland (also for a registered partnership), receive the regular AHV pension or receive a full invalidity pension.
Canton of Zurich: when one of these events occurs, the person is released from the tax-at-source liability from the following month and must fill in a tax return; the tax at source already paid in that year is taken into account in the final tax bill.
Canton of Zurich: on release from the tax-at-source liability the ordinary assessment begins; a tax return is sent to the person, who must fill it in, and who must contact the municipality of residence at once if it does not arrive.
Canton of Zurich: tax at source is due again from the following month when the person separates from or divorces a spouse or registered partner who holds the C permit or a Swiss passport, or when that spouse or partner dies.
ZStB 87.3 margin note 24: a person taxed at source until then is assessed in the ordinary procedure for the whole tax period when they receive the settlement permit or marry a person with Swiss citizenship or the settlement permit; the tax at source is no longer owed from the month after the grant of the permit or the marriage and is credited against the ordinary taxes without interest.

Label: Subsequent ordinary assessment for persons taxed at source in the Canton of Zurich
Description: When a person taxed at source in the Canton of Zurich must file a tax return (CHF 120,000 of gross income, other income or assets), the voluntary request by 31 March and its consequences (Kantonales Steueramt, ZStB 87.3).
Aliases: subsequent ordinary assessment; do I have to file a tax return; tax return tax at source Zurich; gross salary CHF 120000 tax return; pillar 3a deduction tax at source; NOV; Steuererklärung Quellensteuer; Säule 3a Quellensteuer; Antrag bis 31. März Quellensteuer; nachträgliche ordentliche Veranlagung; Bruttolohn; Steuererklärung; Säule 3a; Folgejahres; Schwellenwert; Zweiverdienerehepaare; Die Frist kann nicht verlängert werden; abzugsfähige Aufwendungen; Einkäufe in die berufliche Vorsorge
Questions: I'm a Spanish citizen with a B permit working in Zurich, gross salary CHF 135,000. Tax is deducted at source. Do I have to file a tax return?; Muss ich als quellensteuerpflichtige Person eine Steuererklärung einreichen?
Published facts:
Canton of Zurich: a subsequent ordinary assessment is mandatory for persons taxed at source and resident in Switzerland who earn a gross salary from employment of at least CHF 120,000 a year.
Canton of Zurich: for a tax liability during part of a year, the monthly salary is converted to twelve months to check whether CHF 120,000 is reached, and the gross salaries of spouses are not added together to reach CHF 120,000.
Canton of Zurich: in a subsequent ordinary assessment, the income and wealth taxes are assessed on the completed tax return, and the tax at source already paid is credited without interest against the ordinary federal, cantonal, municipal and church taxes.
Canton of Zurich: persons taxed at source must file a request for a subsequent ordinary assessment if they have other income not subject to tax at source of more than CHF 3,000 or assets of more than CHF 80,000 (CHF 160,000 for persons taxed jointly), or income from self-employment.
Canton of Zurich: persons taxed at source may request a subsequent ordinary assessment to claim deductible expenses that the tax-at-source tariffs do not include or include only as a flat rate, for example actual professional expenses, purchases into the pension fund or pillar 3a contributions.
Canton of Zurich: the request must be filed by 31 March of the following year (the date of electronic submission); the deadline cannot be extended, and when the tax liability ends early, for example on moving abroad, the request must be filed by the deregistration date at the latest.
Canton of Zurich: a request filed on time and in due form cannot be withdrawn, and once it has been filed the person receives a tax return every year, which they must fill in and file.
ZStB 87.3 margin note 13: a subsequent ordinary assessment of the whole income and assets is carried out when the gross income of a person taxed at source reaches or exceeds CHF 120,000 in a tax year; the tax deducted at source is credited without interest.
ZStB 87.3 margin note 13(3): double-earner married couples are subsequently assessed in the ordinary procedure when the gross annual income of one spouse reaches at least CHF 120,000 in a tax year.
ZStB 87.3 margin note 13(4): in the following years, until the tax-at-source liability ends, the subsequent ordinary assessment of the whole income and assets is carried out even if the income falls temporarily or permanently below CHF 120,000.
ZStB 87.3 margin note 15: persons taxed at source who do not reach these thresholds can request a subsequent ordinary assessment from the cantonal tax office by 31 March of the following year; when its conditions are met on request, it is carried out ex officio in the following years until the tax-at-source liability ends.
ZStB 87.3 margin note 15(4): if the request is filed late, the cantonal tax office issues a decision not to consider it, and the tax deducted at source becomes final.

Label: Driving on a foreign licence: federal rules

Label: Health insurance duty on taking up residence
Description: The duty to take out health insurance within three months of taking up residence, cover and premiums from the date of residence, late joining, assignment by the canton and the exemption groups (FOPH).
Aliases: nach dem Umzug krankenversichern; Krankenkasse nach dem Umzug in die Schweiz; sich krankenversichern Frist; health insurance deadline; three months health insurance; too late for health insurance; health insurance after arrival; from when do I pay health insurance premiums; haven't taken out health insurance; Krankenversicherung abschliessen; Krankenkasse Frist; Krankenversicherung ab wann bezahlen; Krankenkasse nach Zuzug; Krankenversicherung ab Einreise; KVG-Versicherungspflicht; drei Monate ab Beginn der Versicherungspflicht; rueckwirkend versichern; verspaetete Anmeldung Praemienzuschlag; Versicherer zuweisen lassen; what happens if I register late for health insurance; how long do I have to take out health insurance; Krankenversicherung; Wohnsitznahme; Versicherungspflicht; Versicherungsschutz; Beitrittsdatum; Prämienzuschlag; rückwirkend; Krankenversicherer; drei Monate; keine Versicherungspflicht; gleichwertigen Versicherungsschutz; take out health insurance; taking up residence; reimbursed retrospectively; authorised health insurer; exempted from the obligation to obtain insurance; solidarisch; Versicherungspflicht nicht mehr untersteht; gemeldeten Wegzugs aus der Schweiz; tatsächlichen Ausreise

Published facts:
FOPH: every person who settles in Switzerland must take out health insurance at the latest three months after taking up residence in Switzerland.
FOPH: on timely joining, cover begins from the date of taking up residence in Switzerland (or of birth); the insurer reimburses costs retroactively to that date, so the insured must also pay the premiums retroactively to that date.
FOPH: on late registration, cover begins only from the date of joining, and an inexcusable delay costs a premium surcharge.
FOPH: if the authority designated by the canton finds that a person has not met the insurance duty in time, it assigns the person to an insurer, and the person cannot choose the insurer.
FOPH: under the coordination of the European social security systems, certain persons may have to take out insurance in an EU/EFTA state or the United Kingdom despite living in Switzerland.
FOPH: insured persons choose freely among the approved health insurers, which must accept them regardless of age and health, without reservations or waiting periods; the application is made directly to the chosen insurer.
FOPH: there is no insurance duty for Swiss or EU/EFTA/UK nationals living in Switzerland who work in an EU/EFTA state or the United Kingdom or receive only a pension from there; for EU/EFTA/UK students in education in Switzerland who do not work; for EU/EFTA/UK nationals posted to Switzerland for up to 24 months; for members of diplomatic or consular missions and staff of international organisations with privileges; and for persons who come to Switzerland only for medical treatment or a cure.
FOPH: exempted on request, if they have equivalent cover for treatment in Switzerland for the whole exemption period, are persons compulsorily insured under the law of a state without an arrangement on the insurance duty for whom Swiss insurance would be a double burden; nationals of a state outside the EU/EFTA/UK in education in Switzerland and their accompanying family; employees posted to Switzerland who are exempt from AHV/IV contributions under an agreement, and their accompanying family; persons living in an EU state who exercise the option right; persons with a residence permit without gainful employment under the free movement or EFTA agreement; and persons for whom Swiss insurance would clearly worsen their cover and who cannot take out supplementary insurance because of age or health. The competent cantonal authorities of the place of residence, stay or work decide on the requests (for pensioners living in an EU/EFTA state or the United Kingdom, the common institution KVG).
The insurance ends when the insured person is no longer subject to the duty to insure.
For foreign nationals with a settlement permit, a short-stay permit or a residence permit the insurance ends on the day of the departure from Switzerland reported to the residents' registration office, in every case on the day of the actual departure from Switzerland, or on the death of the insured person.
Where a child is registered late and the delay is not excusable, the premium surcharge is owed by the parents jointly and severally, or by the one parent, in so far as they are at fault for the delay.

Published facts:
Canton of Zurich: since 1 October 2023, the SVA Zurich is responsible for requests for exemption from the health insurance duty.
SVA Zurich: anyone who lives or works in Switzerland must take out basic insurance under the Health Insurance Act (KVG), as must persons living abroad with a residence permit of at least three months and cross-border commuters; an exemption from the insurance duty is possible in exceptional cases.
SVA Zurich: the most common cases in which an exemption is possible are persons in education or training in Switzerland (students, pupils, trainees) with their accompanying family members, employees posted to Switzerland with their accompanying family members, cross-border commuters, short-stay residents with a permit for at most three months, and persons taxed on a lump sum with a residence permit without gainful employment.
SVA Zurich: an exemption requires proof of foreign insurance cover that pays for treatment in Switzerland at least as the KVG does, without gaps or restrictions in the benefits.
SVA Zurich: a person gainfully employed in Switzerland who has a foreign statutory health insurance (EHIC) cannot be exempted from the insurance duty, apart from exceptional cases for persons living in a country with an option right (Germany, France, Italy or Austria); an exemption with the EHIC is possible only for non-employed persons in education or training, and any work for pay, however low, counts as employment.
SVA Zurich: whoever wants to be exempted from compulsory health insurance in Switzerland must file an application, and SVA Zurich examines the applications in the Canton of Zurich. Depending on the residence status, different persons can be exempted.
SVA Zurich: after the application has been filed, SVA Zurich informs the municipality of residence automatically of its receipt and the applicant has nothing further to do; the application for exemption is then examined. Which supporting documents must be filed depends on the reason for the stay or the residence status, and an online form for the KVG exemption application is provided.

Label: Ordinary naturalisation: federal conditions
Description: The federal conditions of ordinary naturalisation: the C permit, ten years of residence with three of the last five, how permit years count, integration and language, the cantonal minimum residence and the federal fee (SEM).

Questions: I'm a Turkish citizen and have lived in Switzerland for eleven years. I hold a B permit. Can I apply for Swiss citizenship now?; Wann kann ich mich in der Schweiz einbürgern lassen?
Published facts:
SEM: foreign nationals who have lived in Switzerland for ten years and hold the settlement permit C can apply for ordinary naturalisation to the municipality or canton of residence.
SEM: an application for ordinary naturalisation requires 10 years of residence in Switzerland, three of them in the last five years before the application, and a settlement permit (C permit); the years between the 8th and 18th birthday count double, but the actual residence must be at least 6 years (Article 9 of the Swiss Citizenship Act).
SEM: residence counts with a B or C permit and with an FDFA legitimation card or Ci permit; residence with an F permit counts only half; stays during an asylum procedure (N permit) or with a short-stay permit (L permit) do not count.
SEM: the application cannot be filed before the 10 years of residence are complete, because the formal conditions must be met at the time of the application.
SEM: the applicant must be successfully integrated, in particular communicate in everyday life in a national language (oral B1, written A2), respect public security and order (no criminal record entry, no debt enforcement or loss certificates, taxes paid), respect the values of the Federal Constitution, take part in economic life or education (no social assistance in the three years before the application unless fully repaid) and support the integration of family members; the applicant must also be familiar with Swiss living conditions and pose no threat to Switzerland's internal or external security.
SEM: the applicant must prove oral skills at least at reference level B1 and written skills at least at A2 in a Swiss national language (Article 6 of the Citizenship Ordinance); the cantons can require higher language skills.
SEM: cantonal law sets an additional minimum residence of two to five years in the municipality and the canton, and regulates the procedure in the canton and the municipality.
SEM: the application form is available from the competent authority at the place of residence, where the application is also filed.
SEM: for decisions on the federal naturalisation permit, SEM charges CHF 100 for an adult applicant, CHF 150 for spouses applying together and CHF 50 for a minor; municipal and cantonal fees, set by cantonal law, are added.

Label: Ordinary naturalisation in the Canton of Zurich
Description: The Canton of Zurich conditions of ordinary naturalisation (C permit, residence in Switzerland and two years in the same municipality, criminal record, debt enforcement, social assistance, German and basic knowledge), the application to the Gemeindeamt and the fees.

Questions: What are the conditions for naturalisation in the Canton of Zurich?; Wie viele Jahre Wohnsitz in meiner Gemeinde verlangt der Kanton Zürich bei der Einbürgerung?
Published facts:
Canton of Zurich: ordinary naturalisation requires a valid C permit.
Canton of Zurich: at least 10 years of residence in Switzerland are required; years with a C or B permit count fully, years with an F permit half and years with an N or L permit not at all; 3 of the 10 years must fall within the 5 years before the application, and time in Switzerland between the 8th and 18th birthday counts double.
Canton of Zurich: the applicant must have lived in the same municipality for at least 2 years before filing the application; applicants under 25 need only 2 years of residence in the Canton of Zurich before the application.
Canton of Zurich: the applicant has no relevant entries in the criminal record and no pending criminal proceedings.
Canton of Zurich: the applicant must meet important financial obligations and may have no unpaid entries in the debt enforcement register in the last 5 years.
Canton of Zurich: the applicant has received no social assistance in the last 3 years and receives none currently; naturalisation is still possible if it was fully repaid, is needed through no fault of their own for a first formal education, is received by the parents of an applicant under 18, or is received despite full-time work (working poor).
Canton of Zurich: the applicant needs sufficient German skills, at level A2 written and B1 oral.
Canton of Zurich: German skills are proven by a school confirmation, school reports of at least 5 years of compulsory schooling in German, an upper-secondary or tertiary qualification in German or a language certificate; native German speakers need no proof, and applicants without proof must take the cantonal German test (KDE).
Canton of Zurich: the applicant has basic knowledge of the geography, politics, history and society of Switzerland, the Canton of Zurich and the Zurich municipal system; applicants without other proof must take a basic knowledge test.
Canton of Zurich: the application goes to the Gemeindeamt of the Canton of Zurich and passes through a preliminary check by the Gemeindeamt, the examination by the municipality of residence with the grant of municipal citizenship, a new check by the Gemeindeamt with the grant of cantonal citizenship, the examination by SEM with the federal naturalisation permit, and a final check by the Gemeindeamt with the grant of Swiss citizenship; ordinary naturalisation takes about 2 years.
Canton of Zurich: the complete and signed application is sent by A or B post to the Gemeindeamt, Abteilung Einbürgerungen, Wilhelmstrasse 10, 8005 Zürich (postal address Postfach, 8090 Zürich).
Canton of Zurich: an extract from the Swiss civil status register, not older than 6 months when the application is filed, must be submitted; without it the naturalisation cannot be examined.
Canton of Zurich: for ordinary naturalisation the canton charges CHF 500 for applicants over 25, CHF 250 for applicants under 25 and nothing for applicants under 20 (applications from July 2023), who also pay no municipal fee, while applicants under 25 pay half the municipal fee; the Confederation charges CHF 100 (CHF 150 for a married couple, CHF 50 under 18); included children pay nothing; municipal fees differ from municipality to municipality; a rejection costs the municipal fee, CHF 200 at the canton and CHF 300 at the Confederation.

Label: Ordinary naturalisation in the City of Zurich

Questions: I have lived in the city of Zurich for eighteen months. Can I apply for naturalisation there?; Wie lange muss ich in der Stadt Zürich wohnen, bevor ich mich einbürgern lassen kann?
Published facts:
City of Zurich: for ordinary naturalisation the applicant must have lived in the City of Zurich for at least 2 years before filing the application; applicants under 25 need only 2 years of residence in the Canton of Zurich.
City of Zurich: the applicant holds a valid C permit and has lived in Switzerland for 10 years in total; years with a C or B permit count fully, with an F permit half and with an N or L permit not at all; 3 of the 10 years must fall within the 5 years before the application, and time between the 8th and 18th birthday counts double.
City of Zurich: the application is filed online with the Gemeindeamt of the Canton of Zurich, which checks the residence period and forwards it to the City of Zurich; the city examines German skills, basic knowledge of Switzerland, social integration and participation in economic life or education, and may invite the applicant to a personal naturalisation interview.
City of Zurich: ordinary naturalisation must be confirmed by the City of Zurich, the Canton of Zurich and the Confederation, and the procedure takes about 2 years.
City of Zurich: the city charges a fee for ordinary naturalisation; further fees apply for the civil status register extract and, where needed, the proof of German skills, and the Confederation and the canton also charge a fee; for persons in modest economic circumstances the fee can be reduced or waived.
City of Zurich: moving within the City of Zurich is possible at any time during the procedure; moving to another municipality is possible once the city's examination is complete.
City of Zurich: if an applicant does not meet a condition through no fault of their own, for example the required German skills or because they currently receive social assistance, naturalisation may still be possible, and the applicant should contact the city.
City of Zurich: the city's fee for ordinary naturalisation is nothing for applicants under 25 and CHF 500 for applicants over 25.

Label: Facilitated naturalisation of the third generation
Description: Facilitated naturalisation of young foreign nationals whose grandparents came to Switzerland, its conditions, the integration requirement and the application (SEM).
Aliases: third generation naturalisation; born in Switzerland citizenship grandparents; naturalisation before 25; erleichterte Einbürgerung dritte Generation; Einbürgerung Enkel; dritten Generation; Grosselternteil; Niederlassungsbewilligung; obligatorische Schule; 25. Questions: My grandparents came to Switzerland and I was born here. Can I become Swiss more easily?; Welche Bedingungen gelten für die erleichterte Einbürgerung der dritten Generation?
Published facts:
SEM: young foreign nationals whose grandparents came to Switzerland can be naturalised in the facilitated procedure when at least one grandparent was born in Switzerland or is credibly shown to have acquired a right of residence; at least one parent acquired a settlement permit, stayed in Switzerland for at least ten years and attended compulsory school in Switzerland for at least five years; the child was born in Switzerland and holds a settlement permit; and the child attended compulsory school in Switzerland for at least five years. The application is filed before the 25th birthday.
Facilitated naturalisation requires successful integration, which shows in respect for public security and order (for example no tax arrears, debt enforcement, certificates of loss or criminal record entries), respect for the values of the Federal Constitution, the ability to communicate in everyday life in speech and writing in a national language, participation in economic life or in acquiring education (including no social assistance in the three years before the application or its full repayment), and support for the integration of family members. The situation of persons who cannot meet the language or participation criteria because of a disability, an illness or other weighty personal circumstances is taken into account appropriately, and the applicant must not endanger Switzerland's internal or external security.
SEM: a person staying in Switzerland can order the application form directly from the State Secretariat for Migration by e-mail at ch@sem.admin.ch, and submits it fully completed by post to SEM.
SEM: all documents of the list of required documents are submitted together with the application form, its annexes and the signed list itself. SEM provides information forms for the residence right of the grandparents (municipality), juvenile sentences, the social assistance authority, the school authorities and the tax authorities. The State Secretariat for Migration is the competent authority for the facilitated naturalisation of the third generation.

Label: City of Zurich: German for naturalisation
Description: City of Zurich: the German levels required for naturalisation, the accepted certificates, the cantonal German test KDE with its fee, and who needs no proof.
Aliases: German level for Swiss citizenship Zurich; language certificate naturalisation Zurich; KDE test; Deutschtest Einbürgerung Stadt Zürich; Sprachnachweis Einbürgerung; Deutschkenntnisse; Niveau B1; Niveau A2; Sprachzertifikat; Kantonaler Deutsch-Test für die Einbürgerung; Volksschule
Questions: Which German level do I need for naturalisation in the city of Zurich, and which certificates count?; Wie weise ich meine Deutschkenntnisse für die Einbürgerung in der Stadt Zürich nach?
Published facts:
City of Zurich: naturalisation in the city requires German, proven in writing, at level B1 orally (listening and speaking) and level A2 in writing (reading and writing).
City of Zurich: there are two ways to prove German, a language certificate at the required level or the cantonal German test. A certificate must be issued by one of the named institutes (telc, Goethe, the Austrian language diploma ÖSD, TestDaF or the Swiss digital language test SDS).
City of Zurich: an applicant without a language certificate can still file the application and is then asked to sit the cantonal German test for naturalisation (KDE), which has an oral and a written part and whose date and place the city communicates. The applicant bears the cost of the language proof; the KDE costs 250 francs in the city of Zurich.
City of Zurich: no language certificate and no cantonal German test are needed when German is the applicant's mother tongue, when they attended the Volksschule in German for at least five years, when they currently attend compulsory school or upper secondary level in German, when they completed an upper secondary education (for example an apprenticeship) or a tertiary degree in German, when they cannot provide proof for health or psychological reasons, or when they have a reading or learning disability.

Questions: Do I have to take a knowledge test for naturalisation in the city of Zurich, and what is in it?; Was muss ich für den Grundkenntnistest bei der Einbürgerung in Zürich wissen?
Published facts:
City of Zurich: naturalisation in the city requires basic knowledge about Switzerland, which is proven in a test. The applicant must know about Switzerland, the Canton of Zurich and Zurich communal affairs; the test asks questions on geography, politics and history.
City of Zurich: the test of basic knowledge takes place on site at the Stadthaus and is free. The city says when the test can be taken, and it is taken after the naturalisation application has been filed. A learning brochure is sent by post with the invitation and can also be downloaded, and access to a learning app is given at the naturalisation interview.
City of Zurich: no test of basic knowledge is required from applicants who attended compulsory school in Switzerland for at least five years, three of them at lower secondary level; who completed an upper secondary education in Switzerland; or who attend compulsory school or upper secondary level in Switzerland when the application is filed. For persons in the facilitated naturalisation procedure the basic knowledge is checked in the naturalisation interview.

Label: Facilitated naturalisation of the spouse of a Swiss citizen
Description: The federal conditions of facilitated naturalisation for the spouse of a Swiss citizen living in Switzerland: three years of marital community, five years of residence with the last year, integration and language, the application to SEM, exclusions and the fee (SEM).
Aliases: facilitated naturalisation; married to a Swiss citizen citizenship; spouse of a Swiss citizen naturalisation; erleichterte Einbürgerung; erleichtert einbürgern; einbürgern lassen; Schweizer heiraten; mit Schweizer verheiratet; mit einem Schweizer verheiratet; Ehepartner Schweizer Einbürgerung; ohne C-Bewilligung einbürgern; ehelicher Gemeinschaft; Eheschliessung; eingetragenen Partnerschaft; Referenzniveau A2; Landessprache; Gesuchsformular; Staatssekretariat für Migration; Sozialhilfe; Integration; simplified naturalisation; successfully integrated
Questions: Ich bin seit vier Jahren mit einem Schweizer verheiratet und habe eine B-Bewilligung. Kann ich mich erleichtert einbürgern lassen, obwohl ich keine C-Bewilligung habe?; I have been married to a Swiss citizen for four years and hold a B permit. Can I apply for facilitated naturalisation?
Published facts:
SEM: the husband or wife of a Swiss citizen can apply for facilitated naturalisation if they have stayed in Switzerland for five years in total, spent the last year before filing the application in Switzerland and have lived in marital community with the Swiss spouse for three years.
SEM: facilitated naturalisation of the foreign spouse is excluded if both spouses were foreign nationals at the time of the marriage and the spouse acquired Swiss citizenship by ordinary naturalisation after the marriage, or if the Swiss spouse has died before the application is filed.
SEM: facilitated naturalisation requires successful integration, shown in particular by respecting public security and order (for example no tax arrears, debt enforcement, loss certificates or criminal record entries), respecting the values of the Federal Constitution, communicating in a national language in everyday life, taking part in economic life or education (including no social assistance in the three years before the application, or its full repayment) and supporting the integration of family members; the applicant must not endanger Switzerland's internal or external security.
SEM: an applicant living in Switzerland must prove, when filing the application, written language skills at least at reference level A2 and oral skills at least at B1 in a Swiss national language.
SEM: an applicant living in Switzerland orders the application form directly from SEM by e-mail (ch@sem.admin.ch) and files the completed form with SEM by post.
SEM decides on facilitated naturalisation.
SEM: a person in a registered partnership with a Swiss citizen cannot apply for facilitated naturalisation; registered partners can only apply for ordinary naturalisation, and facilitated naturalisation is open only to married couples.
SEM: facilitated naturalisation is not possible if the spouse was naturalised after the marriage in the ordinary procedure or as a foreign national of the third generation; it is possible if the spouse acquired Swiss citizenship after the marriage by reinstatement or by facilitated naturalisation based on descent from a Swiss parent.
SEM: facilitated naturalisation of spouses of Swiss citizens living in Switzerland costs CHF 900, paid in advance and not refunded if the application is rejected.

Label: Facilitated naturalisation in the Canton of Zurich
Description: Facilitated naturalisation as the Canton of Zurich describes it: the spouse who was Swiss at the marriage, the conditions, the application to SEM, the steps and duration, and the SEM fee.
Aliases: facilitated naturalisation Zurich; erleichterte Einbürgerung Kanton Zürich; Einbürgerung Ehepartner Zürich; erleichterte Einbürgerung; Heirat; Heimatorte; Gesuchsformular; Staatssekretariat für Migration; Gemeindeamt; Landessprache
Questions: How does facilitated naturalisation work in the Canton of Zurich?; Wie läuft die erleichterte Einbürgerung von Ehepartnern im Kanton Zürich ab?
Published facts:
Canton of Zurich: facilitated naturalisation is possible for a person married to a Swiss citizen who was already Swiss at the time of the marriage; if the spouse was naturalised in the ordinary procedure, proof of the places of origin must be submitted with the application.
Canton of Zurich: the application form is ordered directly from SEM (ch@sem.admin.ch), and the application with the completed documents is sent by post to the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM).
Canton of Zurich: the application passes through a preliminary check by SEM, an examination by the Gemeindeamt (canton), an examination by the municipality, a new examination by the Gemeindeamt and a final examination by SEM with the grant of Swiss citizenship; facilitated naturalisation takes about 2 years.
Canton of Zurich: an application can be filed when the applicant has no unpaid debt enforcement, has paid the final tax bills, has no criminal record entries, respects the values of the Federal Constitution, speaks and writes a national language, is financially independent, supports the family's integration, has basic knowledge of Switzerland, takes part in social and cultural life and does not endanger Switzerland's internal or external security.
Canton of Zurich: SEM charges a fee of CHF 900 for facilitated naturalisation, CHF 650 for persons under 18.

Questions: I live in the city of Zurich and am married to a Swiss citizen. Where do I apply for facilitated naturalisation?; Wo reiche ich in der Stadt Zürich das Gesuch um erleichterte Einbürgerung ein?
Published facts:
City of Zurich: facilitated naturalisation applies, among others, to a person married for at least 3 years to a Swiss citizen who was already Swiss at the time of the marriage.
City of Zurich: SEM is responsible for facilitated naturalisation; it must be confirmed by the City of Zurich, the Canton of Zurich and the Confederation, and the procedure takes about 2 years.
City of Zurich: the application is filed by post with SEM, which checks completeness and the formal conditions and forwards it to the Canton of Zurich; the Gemeindeamt checks the criminal record, the City of Zurich examines integration in an interview on behalf of the canton and writes a report, and SEM decides on the naturalisation.
City of Zurich: the application form can be ordered free of charge from the City of Zurich through its contact form; the completed application and documents are then sent by post to SEM, Quellenweg 6, 3003 Bern-Wabern.
City of Zurich: the applicant needs skills in at least one national language (German, French, Italian or Romansh) at level A2 written and B1 oral.
City of Zurich: SEM charges a fee for facilitated naturalisation.
City of Zurich page on facilitated naturalisation: the SEM's fee is CHF 650 for applicants under 18 and CHF 900 for applicants over 18.

Label: City of Zurich: city citizenship for Swiss citizens
Description: City of Zurich: how a Swiss citizen applies for the city citizenship, the two years of residence, the documents, the fee and the procedure.
Aliases: city citizenship Zurich Swiss; Bürgerrecht der Stadt Zürich; Stadtbürgerrecht beantragen; second communal citizenship; Stadtbürgerrecht; Gemeindebürgerrecht; Betreibungsregister; Personenstandsausweis; Stadtkanzlei; AGOV
Questions: I am Swiss and live in Zurich. How do I apply for the city citizenship?; Wie beantrage ich als Schweizerin das Stadtbürgerrecht der Stadt Zürich?
Published facts:
City of Zurich: Swiss citizens can apply for the city citizenship of Zurich when they have lived in the city without interruption for at least two years. The application needs the application form and, depending on the personal situation, further documents; it usually takes about three months and costs 200 francs, and is free for persons under 25. The existing communal citizenship does not have to be given up, because the Canton of Zurich allows several communal citizenships, but the applicant should clarify beforehand with the authority of their canton of origin whether several are allowed there.
City of Zurich: the city citizenship can be applied for when the applicant has lived in the city of Zurich without interruption for at least two years and has no entries in the criminal record and no pending criminal proceedings.
City of Zurich: the documents for the application are an extract from the debt enforcement register (from the debt enforcement office of the current or former city district or former municipality of residence), a civil status certificate (one extract is enough even with several places of origin), an extract from the criminal record (from a post office counter or online at strafregister.admin.ch), a copy of the divorce decree where minor children of an earlier marriage are included, a declaration of consent of parents with custody who are not named in the application (naturalising a minor child needs the consent of both parents with custody), proof of parental custody where minor children of unmarried or divorced parents are included, and a power of attorney where the application is filed for someone else.
City of Zurich: the application can be filed online or by post once all documents are together. Filing online requires a confirmed identity through an AGOV login, the official login for Swiss authority services, which private individuals can set up free of charge; the guided online submission takes about ten minutes with the documents at hand. By post, the form "Gesuch um Aufnahme von Schweizer Bürger*innen in das Stadtbürgerrecht" is completed, signed and sent with all documents. The Stadtkanzlei examines the application and prepares the request for the city council. Processing usually takes about three months and can differ with the individual case and the completeness of the documents; the fee is 200 francs and the procedure is free for persons under 25.

Label: City of Zurich: where a particular item goes
Description: City of Zurich: which collection takes electrical appliances, mirrors and drinking glasses, bulky goods, metal, hazardous waste, lamps and plastics, and the disposal app and calendar.
Aliases: where do I throw away a mirror Zurich; dispose of old furniture Zurich; drinking glass not in glass collection; Sperrgut Zürich; Grubengut; Sonderabfall entsorgen Zürich; Sperrgut; Sonderabfall; Wertstoff-Sammelstellen; Züri-Sack; Kleinmetall
Questions: Where do I dispose of a broken mirror, an old toaster and a mattress in the city of Zurich?; Wohin gehören Trinkgläser und Spiegel in der Stadt Zürich?
Published facts:
City of Zurich: electrical appliances such as toasters, irons, hairdryers, televisions, radios, electric drills, computers and smartphones contain recyclable metals and toxic heavy metals and are collected separately; Entsorgung + Recycling Zürich also collects them from home for a charge.
City of Zurich: mirrors, window glass and furniture glass are so-called Grubengut, waste with glass-like or stone-like components, and so are drinking glasses, cups and other crockery, vases of glass, ceramic, porcelain and clay, and flower pots. Drinking glasses do not belong in the glass collection because they usually contain more lead. A mirror of at most one metre by one metre can also be given to Entsorgung + Recycling Zürich for collection for a charge, and a single drinking glass or cup can go into the household waste in the Züri-Sack.
City of Zurich: furniture, mattresses, carpets, suitcases and wickerwork are bulky goods (Sperrgut), combustible waste too big and too heavy for the Züri-Sack. Metal shelves and other larger metal objects such as bicycles and grills are large metal; small metal such as tins, drink cans, small pans, screws, wires and aluminium foil can be taken to the recyclable material collection points free of charge. Garden shears usually count as large metal, with foreign material such as plastic or wood removed where possible, while small shears that fit through the container opening of 4 by 18 centimetres can go to the collection points.
City of Zurich: hazardous waste such as spray cans, paints and varnishes, partly recognisable by the danger symbol, is harmful and dangerous and must not go into household waste but is collected separately. Lamps (energy-saving lamps, LED lamps, fluorescent tubes) are hazardous waste too; ordinary light bulbs, which are hardly in circulation any more, can go into the household waste and are also accepted at the hazardous waste collection points in case of doubt.
City of Zurich: PET drink bottles belong in the PET collection containers or can be returned to retailers free of charge; other plastic bottles can be collected separately and are usually taken back free of charge by retailers, or disposed of at ERZ. Other plastics such as cups, food packaging and carrier bags can go into special plastic collection bags or into the household waste. The free Entsorgung + Recycling Zürich app holds the information on all the waste groups, and a personal disposal calendar can be put together online as a printable PDF.

Questions: How do I get to the SVA Zurich and when is it open?; Hat die SVA Zürich an Feiertagen offen?
Published facts:
SVA Zurich: the public customer service (Öffentlicher Kundendienst) is at Röntgenstrasse 17, 8005 Zürich, open Monday to Friday from 8.00 to 17.00 without appointment; coming in the morning shortens waiting times, and advice is given in German and, where possible, in other languages.
SVA Zurich: the office is a few minutes' walk from Zurich main station, in District 5 next to the SBB tracks. By tram, take line 17 (towards Werdhölzli), 50 (towards Frankental) or 51 (towards Bahnhof Altstetten Nord) from the stop Sihlquai/HB to Limmatplatz, then bus 32 (towards Strassenverkehrsamt/Albisgüetli) to the first stop, Röntgenstrasse, or walk five minutes along Langstrasse. On foot from the main station (exit Sihlquai) along Zollstrasse it takes about ten minutes. By car it is near the Hardturm, Letten and Wiedikon motorway feeders, signposted from Escher-Wyss-Platz; public transport is preferred because parking nearby is paid and time-limited.
SVA Zurich: the SVA can be reached by telephone Monday to Friday from 8.00 to 17.00; calling at lunchtime or at the edges of the day avoids long queues, a callback service is offered in some cases, and callers should have their AHV number (on the back of the health insurance card) or, for companies and the self-employed, their account number, shown on every AHV contribution invoice, ready.

Canton of Zurich: every dog keeper needs liability insurance covering at least CHF 1 million, whatever the dog's size or breed, and pays an annual dog tax for each dog to the municipality of residence.
Canton of Zurich: since 1 June 2025, anyone living in a Zurich municipality who keeps a dog for at least three months must complete a theory and a practical training with a trainer licensed by the Veterinary Office; this also applies to people who move into the canton with their dog.
Canton of Zurich: the theory course, which ends with a test and lasts about two hours on average, may be taken at the earliest one year before and must be taken at the latest two months after starting to keep a dog or moving into the canton. Label: Who needs a visa to enter Switzerland
Description: Whether a visa is needed depends on nationality; SEM's list by nationality, the visa requirement of the VEV for short and longer stays, and the states exempt from the long-stay visa.
Aliases: do I need a visa for Switzerland; visa requirement by nationality; visa free Switzerland; third country national visa; brauche ich ein Visum; Visumpflicht Schweiz; visumfrei einreisen; Liste Visumvorschriften; Drittstaaten; Visumvorschriften nach Staatsangehörigkeit; Anhang CH-1; Visumpflicht für kurzfristige Aufenthalte; Visumpflicht für längerfristige Aufenthalte; Schengen-Visa; visa provisions according to nationality; Annex CH-1
Questions: Do I need a visa to enter Switzerland?; Brauche ich ein Visum für die Schweiz?; Which nationalities do not need a visa for a long stay?
Published facts:
SEM: whether you need a visa to enter Switzerland depends on your nationality. The rules per nationality are published in the overview of identity-document and visa requirements by nationality (Annex CH-1, List 1). Third countries are states that do not belong to the European Union and/or the Schengen area.
VEV Article 8: nationals of the states listed in Annex I of EU Regulation 2018/1806 need a visa for short stays. Exempt are, among others, holders of a recognised and valid travel document together with a long-stay visa or a valid residence title issued by a Schengen state.
VEV Article 9: third-country nationals need a Swiss long-stay visa for a stay of more than 90 days. Holders of a long-stay visa or a valid residence title of another Schengen state are exempt, as are nationals of Andorra, Australia, Brunei Darussalam, Japan, Malaysia, Monaco, New Zealand, San Marino, Singapore, Vatican City and the United Kingdom.
SEM: Schengen visas are valid for Switzerland and for the whole Schengen area, unless the visa says otherwise.

Label: Schengen visa (type C) and national visa (type D)
Description: The two visa types a Swiss representation issues: the Schengen visa C for stays of up to 90 days in 180 and the national visa D for stays of more than 90 days, which needs the cantonal migration office's approval.
Aliases: Schengen visa; type C visa; type D visa; national visa Switzerland; long stay visa; which visa do I need; Schengenvisum; nationales Visum; Visum Typ C; Visum Typ D; Schengenvisum Typ C; Nationales Visum Typ D; Visum C; Visum D; kantonalen Migrationsamts; Arbeitsbewilligung; Familiennachzug; category C visa; category D visa; multiple-entry
Questions: What is the difference between a type C and a type D visa?; Which visa do I need to work in Switzerland?; Welches Visum brauche ich?
Published facts:
FDFA: since the Schengen and Dublin association agreement between Switzerland and the EU entered into force (12 December 2008), the representations abroad issue two kinds of visa depending on the purpose of stay: the Schengen visa type C for short entries and stays of at most 90 days within 180 days, and the national visa type D for long-term, permit-based stays of more than 90 days.
SEM: a type C visa is issued for stays of at most 90 days within a period of 180 days, is valid for the whole Schengen area and is also called a Schengen visa. It covers tourism, visits to relatives or friends, sporting or cultural events, business, and school or studies. For a stay with gainful employment a separate work permit is needed in addition to a valid type C visa.
SEM: a type D visa is issued for stays of more than 90 days and is also called a national visa. It is needed for gainful employment, education or further education, and family reunification.
FDFA: a national visa type D is granted only with the approval of the cantonal migration office responsible for the intended place of residence in Switzerland.
SEM: a Schengen visa can be issued for one, two or several entries and can be valid for up to five years. The competent representation abroad decides the period of validity and the number of entries case by case, on the reasons for the journey and the documents submitted.

Label: How long a short stay may last: 90 days in any 180
Description: The short-stay rule of the Schengen area: at most 90 days within any 180 days, counted over a rolling window with the days of entry and exit included, and what applies after a residence permit expires.
Aliases: 90 days in 180 days; how long can I stay in Switzerland; Schengen 90 180 rule; rolling 180 days; overstay Schengen; 90 Tage Regel; Aufenthaltsdauer berechnen; wie lange darf ich bleiben; how many days am I allowed in the Schengen area; 90 Tage innerhalb von 180 Tagen; gleitender; Tag der Einreise; Schengen-Raum; Bezugszeitraum von 180 Tagen; 90 days within a 180-day period; 180-day period; Earliest re-entry
Questions: How long can I stay in Switzerland without a permit?; How is the 90 days in 180 days calculated?; Wie wird die Aufenthaltsdauer berechnet?
Published facts:
SEM: third-country nationals may in principle enter the Schengen area for at most 90 days within 180 days. Where a visa is required, the duration noted on the visa applies. The day of entry counts as the first day in the Schengen area and the day of departure as the last. The 180 days are a rolling period: on any given day one looks back over the last 180 days and may have spent at most 90 of them in the Schengen area. After 90 days spent outside the Schengen area, one may enter again for up to 90 days.
SEM's example of 90 consecutive days: entry on 1 March (day 1), stay until 29 May (90 days), departure on 29 May as day 90. The traveller must then stay outside the Schengen area for 90 days, from 29 May to 27 August; the earliest re-entry is 28 August, when a new period begins.
SEM: for stays longer than 90 days within 180 days, third-country nationals need a residence permit; permits are granted by the cantonal authority of the place of residence.
SEM: persons exempt from the visa requirement may stay in Switzerland for a further 90 consecutive days without a permit after their residence permit has expired. Before travelling to another Schengen state they should ask that state's authorities whether and on what terms a stay is allowed.
SEM: 25 states of the European Union and four states of the European Free Trade Association form the Schengen area, where the uniform rule for short stays of at most 90 days per reference period of 180 days applies.

Label: Entry requirements for third-country nationals
Description: What a visa-required third-country national must have at the border: a visa or residence title, a recognised travel document, the purpose of the stay, sufficient means of subsistence, and no SIS alert or expulsion order.
Aliases: entry requirements Switzerland; what do I need at the border; sufficient funds Switzerland; money per day Switzerland; invitation letter Switzerland; Einreisevoraussetzungen; finanzielle Mittel Einreise; Verpflichtungserklärung; anerkannten Reisedokuments; ausreichende finanzielle Mittel; Schengener Informationssystem; Einladungsschreiben; Einreisevoraussetzungen für kurzfristige Aufenthalte; recognized travel document; Schengen Information System
Questions: What do I need to enter Switzerland as a third-country national?; How much money must I show at the Swiss border?; Was sind genügende finanzielle Mittel?
Published facts:
SEM: visa-required third-country nationals must hold a valid type C (Schengen) visa, a valid type D (national) visa or a valid residence title of a Schengen state; hold a recognised travel document issued less than ten years ago and valid at least three months beyond the intended departure from the Schengen area (type C) or until departure (type D and residence titles); show the purpose and circumstances of the stay; have sufficient financial means for the stay and the return or transit journey, or be able to acquire them lawfully; not be listed in the Schengen Information System (SIS) for refusal of entry; pose no danger to public order, internal security, public health or the international relations of a Schengen state; and not have been sentenced to expulsion or a measure to keep them away.
SEM: third-country nationals staying in Switzerland at their own expense must show CHF 100 per day of stay; the guide value for students with a valid student card is CHF 30 per day. The means can be shown with cash, traveller's cheques, credit cards or other security such as a bank guarantee. Border authorities may ask about the purpose of the stay and the financial means and may refuse entry when the person has insufficient means or gives no information. A person without sufficient means can enter Switzerland with a host's letter of invitation.
VEV Article 3: the entry requirements for short stays follow Article 6 of the Schengen Borders Code. Means of subsistence count as sufficient in particular when it is assured that no social assistance will be drawn during the stay in the Schengen area. Proof can be provided with cash, a bank balance, a declaration of sponsorship (Verpflichtungserklärung) or another security.
VEV Article 4: for a longer stay, foreign nationals must in addition to Article 6(1)(a), (d) and (e) of the Schengen Borders Code hold a long-stay visa under Article 9 where one is required, and meet the admission requirements of foreign-nationals law for the intended purpose of stay.

Label: Entry requirements for EU/EFTA nationals and their family members
Description: What EU and EFTA nationals need at the Swiss border, what their third-country family members need, and who counts as a family member.

Questions: What documents does an EU citizen need to enter Switzerland?; Does my non-EU spouse need a visa if I am an EU citizen?; Wer gilt als Familienangehöriger einer EU-Bürgerin?
Published facts:
SEM: EU and EFTA nationals must present a personal identity document, an identity card or a passport; depending on nationality Switzerland also recognises expired travel documents for crossing the border. They must pose no danger to public order, internal security, public health or the international relations of a Schengen state, and must not have been sentenced to expulsion or a measure to keep them away.
SEM: third-country nationals who are family members of an EU or EFTA national must hold a valid type C (Schengen) visa if they come from a country subject to the visa requirement; hold a recognised travel document valid at least three months beyond the intended departure from the Schengen area and issued less than ten years ago; hold a valid residence title of a Schengen member state or a visa where needed; not be listed in the Schengen Information System (SIS) for refusal of entry; pose no danger to public order, internal security, public health or international relations; and not have been sentenced to expulsion or a measure to keep them away.
SEM: family members of EU and EFTA nationals are, whatever their own nationality, the spouse or the partner of a registered partnership based on the law of a member state and treated as equal to marriage there and in the host member state; the direct descendants of the EU/EFTA national and of the spouse or registered partner who are under 21 or dependent; and the dependent direct ascendants of the EU/EFTA national and of the spouse or registered partner, for example parents or grandparents.
SEM: Swiss citizens have a right to enter Switzerland and must prove or credibly show their Swiss citizenship when crossing the border. Recommended documents are a valid Swiss passport or identity card, a photocopy of either, an expired travel document, or an official document showing identity and/or citizenship such as a driving licence.

Label: Where and how to apply for a Swiss visa
Description: The Swiss representation abroad issues visas, not SEM: where the application goes, when to file it, the application forms, and how a type D application reaches the cantonal migration office.
Aliases: how to apply for a Swiss visa; where to apply visa Switzerland; visa application form Switzerland; Swiss embassy visa; Visum beantragen; Visumantrag stellen; Schweizer Vertretung; Auslandvertretungen; Visumantragsformular; zuständigen Schweizer Vertretung; Hauptreiseziels; kantonale Migrationsamt; Swiss representations abroad; main destination
Questions: Where do I apply for a Swiss visa?; How early can I apply for a Schengen visa?; Wo und wie beantrage ich ein Visum D?
Published facts:
SEM: SEM does not issue visas. The Swiss representations abroad are responsible for granting and refusing visas.
SEM: applications for a type C visa must be submitted online, in writing on the application form, or directly to the Swiss representation responsible for the applicant's place of residence. The application can be filed six months before the planned journey and should ideally be filed at the latest two months before departure.
SEM: a type D visa must be applied for in writing on the application form or directly at the Swiss representation responsible for the applicant's place of residence. A stay of more than 90 days in Switzerland needs a permit, so the representation forwards the visa application to the cantonal migration office for examination. Questions about the stay and the permit go to the cantonal migration and labour-market authorities, questions about the visa application and its documents to the representation.
SEM: when only one member state is the destination, the consulate of that state is competent for the visa application. When the journey covers several destinations, the consulate of the main destination is competent, which is as a rule the longest stay.
SEM publishes the visa application forms in several languages: the Schengen application form for short stays of at most three months within six months in the whole Schengen area, for example tourism or visits, and the application form for a national type D visa for long-term, permit-based stays in Switzerland from three months, for example gainful employment or family reunification. Further application forms in local languages are on the websites of the Swiss representations abroad.
FDFA: the application should be filed early, because processing can take several weeks to months depending on the season and the type of visa. A Schengen visa application can be filed at the earliest six months before the planned entry into the Schengen area. The documents to be submitted and the procedure depend on the applicant's country of residence; the country pages give the conditions.

Label: Visa fee, travel health insurance and processing time
Description: What a Swiss visa costs, who is exempt, the travel health insurance a type C applicant must show, and how long a decision takes.
Aliases: Swiss visa cost; Schengen visa fee; visa processing time Switzerland; travel insurance Schengen visa; visa free of charge; Visumgebühr; Visum Kosten; Bearbeitungszeit Visum; Reisekrankenversicherung; Dienstleistungsgebühr; gebührenfrei; Visumverfahren; visa fee; external service provider; medical insurance
Questions: How much does a Swiss visa cost?; How long does a Swiss visa application take?; What travel insurance do I need for a Schengen visa?; Welche Gebühr und welche Reisekrankenversicherung verlangt ein Visumgesuch?
Published facts:
SEM: a fee is charged for filing a visa application, EUR 90 for adults and EUR 45 for children between 6 and 12 years. No surcharges may be asked for Schengen visas; for certain applicants a visa may be issued free of charge. At most locations applications are filed with an external service provider, which charges a service fee on top of the visa fee. For national visas (stays of more than 90 days) a surcharge of up to 50 per cent of the fee may be charged for urgent services, services outside normal working hours, and procedures of unusual size or difficulty.
SEM: visas for family members of EU/EFTA citizens are issued free of charge.
SEM: whoever applies for a type C visa must show travel health insurance for the whole duration of the stay, covering up to EUR 30,000 of the costs of repatriation for medical reasons, emergency medical care, emergency hospital treatment and death, including repatriation of the remains. For several stays, insurance must be shown for the first stay and the applicant signs a declaration that adequate insurance will also be taken out for the further stays.
SEM: once a Swiss representation considers a type C visa application admissible (application, travel document, photograph and other relevant documents filed, fingerprints taken and the visa fee collected), it decides as a rule within 15 days; in exceptional cases the period can be extended to 30 or even 60 days. Applications for a national type D visa fall under cantonal competence; the processing time varies from canton to canton and by purpose of stay, and as a rule at least one month must be reckoned with.

Label: ETIAS travel authorisation
Description: The European travel authorisation for visa-free travellers: who needs it, how long it is valid, what it costs and that at the time of the cited page no applications could yet be filed.
Aliases: ETIAS; travel authorisation Europe; do I need ETIAS for Switzerland; ETIAS cost; ETIAS validity; ETIAS Schweiz; Reisegenehmigung Europa; ETIAS beantragen; ETIAS-Reisegenehmigung; Reisegenehmigungssystem; visumsbefreit; Kurzaufenthalt; European Travel Information and Authorisation System; visa-exempt; ETIAS travel authorisation
Questions: Do I need an ETIAS to travel to Switzerland?; How much does ETIAS cost and how long is it valid?; Kann ich ETIAS schon beantragen?
Published facts:
SEM: ETIAS, short for European Travel Information and Authorisation System, is the new European travel authorisation system for nationals of 59 countries who travel visa-free for a short stay (less than 90 days within a period of 180 days) to one of 30 European countries.
SEM, on the page saved on 11 September 2026: the European Union sets the timetable for introducing ETIAS, applications cannot yet be filed and travellers need take no steps for the time being. The EU will announce the exact date a few months before ETIAS enters into force.
SEM: an ETIAS travel authorisation is tied to the passport given in the application form and is valid for up to three years or until that travel document expires. With a valid authorisation travellers may enter the 30 European countries as often as they wish, as long as they do not exceed 90 days within a period of 180 days. The authorisation does not guarantee entry: the entry conditions are still checked at the border.
SEM: travellers will have to apply for a chargeable ETIAS travel authorisation on the European Union's website or app before travelling to the Schengen area. They need a passport valid for at least three more months, a credit card and an e-mail address. It will cost EUR 20, and some travellers are exempt from the fee.
SEM: most ETIAS applications are processed automatically within minutes. In individual cases the check takes longer and a decision follows within four days; that period can be extended to 14 days when the competent authority asks for additional information or documents, so it is advisable to apply in good time.

Label: The Entry/Exit System (EES) at the Schengen border
Description: The system that records entries and exits of third-country nationals electronically, calculates the duration of stay and replaces the stamping of travel documents.
Aliases: EES; Entry Exit System; passport stamp Schengen; biometric border control; fingerprints border; Einreise Ausreise System; Stempel Reisepass; Grenzkontrolle biometrisch; Entry/Exit System; Abstempelung; Aufenthaltsdauer; Drittstaatsangehörigen; Schengen-Aussengrenzen
Questions: What is the Entry/Exit System?; Is my passport still stamped when I enter Switzerland?; Welche Daten erfasst das EES?
Published facts:
SEM: the Entry/Exit System (EES) has been introduced gradually across the Schengen area since 12 October 2025. Travellers are asked to inform themselves on the European Commission's official EES website.
SEM: the EES is a system for managing the Schengen external borders. It records the entries and exits of third-country nationals electronically and calculates the duration of stay in the Schengen area automatically. The manual stamping of travel documents is replaced by an entry in the EES. The system is to make irregular migration, in particular overstayers, easier to detect and undocumented travellers easier to identify, among other things with biometric identifiers (facial image and four fingerprints).

Label: Voting rights: federal rules
Description: Who may vote and elect in Switzerland: political rights in federal matters belong to Swiss citizens aged 18 or over; foreign nationals, whatever their permit or length of stay, cannot vote or elect at federal level, and only some cantons and communes give them a vote in cantonal or communal matters; automatic entry in the electoral register and dual citizens (Federal Constitution Art. 39 and 136, ch.ch).
