Questions: Can foreign nationals vote in Switzerland?; I have had a C permit for twelve years. Am I allowed to vote in federal elections?; Darf ich als Ausländer in der Schweiz abstimmen?
Published facts:
Political rights in federal matters belong to all Swiss citizens aged 18 or over who are not excluded for mental incapacity; all have the same political rights and duties.
Swiss citizens with political rights can take part in National Council elections and federal votes, and can launch and sign popular initiatives and referendums in federal matters.
Foreign nationals can neither vote nor elect at federal level. Depending on the canton and the commune, foreign nationals may have the right to vote and elect at cantonal and communal level; not every canton grants it.
At cantonal level, the cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel give foreign nationals the right to vote and elect, but not the right to stand for election.
The Confederation regulates the exercise of political rights in federal matters; the cantons regulate it in cantonal and communal matters. Political rights are exercised at the place of residence, and no one may exercise them in more than one canton.
Swiss citizens aged 18 or over who live in Switzerland can take part in federal, cantonal and communal votes and elections. They do not need to register: the municipality of residence enters them in the electoral register automatically when they meet the conditions.
Dual citizenship does not affect the right to vote: a Swiss citizen with another nationality votes and elects like every other Swiss citizen.

Label: Pillar 3a private pension
Description: Explains who may open and pay into the restricted private pension (pillar 3a), the annual contribution limits and tax deduction, when the savings can be withdrawn including on permanently leaving Switzerland, and how pillar 3a differs from unrestricted pillar 3b savings (FSIO, ch.ch).
Aliases: pillar 3a; Säule 3a; private pension Switzerland; private Vorsorge; gebundene Selbstvorsorge; 3a vs 3b; tax deduction pillar 3a; when can I withdraw pillar 3a; leaving Switzerland pillar 3a; maximum contribution pillar 3a; Säule 3a einzahlen; AHV-pflichtiges Einkommen; Pensionskasse; Vorsorgeeinrichtung; steuerlich abziehbar; ungebundene Selbstvorsorge; Wohneigentum; Kapitalbezug; Sparguthaben; einzahlen
Questions: How much can I pay into pillar 3a this year?; Wann kann ich mein Säule-3a-Guthaben beziehen, wenn ich die Schweiz endgültig verlasse?; What is the difference between pillar 3a and pillar 3b?
Published facts:
A person can set up and pay into a pillar 3a if they have an income subject to AHV contributions as an employee or a self-employed person. A person who lives abroad but works in Switzerland and is insured under the AHV can also set up a pillar 3a, as can a person receiving daily allowances from Swiss unemployment insurance, and a person receiving a federal disability insurance (IV) pension who continues a partial gainful activity with AHV-liable income.
A person can continue paying into pillar 3a up to five years after their 65th birthday if they keep working beyond the ordinary retirement age. They can also continue paying in during a temporary interruption of gainful activity, for example civil or military service, unemployment, or illness.
In 2026, an employee who belongs to a pension fund (2nd pillar) may pay a maximum of CHF 7,258 per year into pillar 3a. A self-employed person with no pension fund, or an employee not affiliated to any pension scheme, may pay up to 20 percent of their annual income, to a maximum of CHF 36,288 per year.
Amounts paid into pillar 3a are deductible from taxes; the payments can be deducted from the annual tax return each year they are made.
Pillar 3a is restricted retirement savings held with a bank or insurance company: a maximum amount can be paid in each year, interest is higher than on a savings account, contributions are tax deductible, withdrawal is subject to conditions, and a one-time tax based on income at the time of withdrawal applies when the funds are paid out. Pillar 3b is unrestricted savings such as cash, a savings passbook, life insurance or investments: any amount may be paid in each year, the saved capital must generally be declared and taxed annually, and it can be withdrawn at any time without an additional tax.
Pillar 3a savings can normally be paid out at retirement, or at the earliest five years before the ordinary AHV retirement age of 65.
Early lump-sum withdrawal of pillar 3a savings is possible only in specific cases: buying or building owner-occupied housing, permanently leaving Switzerland, taking up self-employment or a new self-employed activity, buying additional contribution years in a 2nd pillar pension fund, or receiving a full IV disability pension where the disability risk is not insured.
A person who decides to work beyond the ordinary retirement age of 65 can keep paying into pillar 3a and defer the withdrawal by up to five years. When the savings are withdrawn, the entire pillar 3a balance must be paid out at once.

Label: Unemployment benefit
Description: Explains who is insured against unemployment, the eligibility conditions for unemployment benefit (ALE), how and when to sign on with the RAV, and how the amount and duration of the benefit are set (SECO / arbeit.swiss).
Aliases: unemployment benefit; Arbeitslosenentschädigung; who is insured against unemployment; RAV registration; beim RAV anmelden; how much unemployment pay; wie viel Arbeitslosengeld; 12 months contribution unemployment; residence permit unemployment benefit; Job-Room registrieren; lost my job; Stelle verloren; Job verloren; Rahmenfrist für die Beitragszeit; Beitragszeit; Niederlassungs- oder Aufenthaltsbewilligung; Job-Room; Grenzgänger; versicherten Verdienstes; Erstgespräch; PD U2; eService; regional employment centre; qualifying period for contributions; insured salary; public employment service
Questions: How do I sign on with the RAV if I lose my job?; Wie viel Arbeitslosenentschädigung bekomme ich und wie lange?; Can a foreign national with a residence permit claim unemployment benefit in Switzerland?
Published facts:
Almost the entire employed population of Switzerland is compulsorily insured against unemployment, and liability to contribute follows the federal AHV law; earnings are insured under unemployment insurance (ALV) once they average at least CHF 500 per month. Self-employed persons are not insured.
An employee is not entitled to unemployment benefit while, as a board member of a stock corporation, a partner in a GmbH, a person financially involved in the business, or a member of the company's supreme decision-making body, they can determine or materially influence the employer's decisions; the same exclusion applies to their working spouse, registered partner or civil partner.
To claim unemployment benefit, a person must be fully or partly unemployed; someone with a part-time job who is looking for a full-time or another part-time position is also insured. A person only counts as unemployed once they have registered with the placement service, either via arbeit.swiss or in person at their RAV, and they must have lost at least 2 days of work with a corresponding loss of earnings.
A claimant must live in Switzerland; a foreign national must hold a valid settlement or residence permit. A person who lives abroad but worked in Switzerland (a cross-border commuter) generally claims unemployment benefit in their country of residence, under the rules that apply there.
A claimant must prove at least 12 months of contribution period within the last 2 years before registering (the contribution period frame). This 2-year frame can be extended under certain conditions, which are examined when the claimant gave up a self-employed activity or was raising children under 10 years old.
A person is also insured without having completed the ordinary contribution period if, for a total of more than 12 months, they could not be in employment because of education (provided they lived in Switzerland for at least 10 years), illness, accident or maternity (provided they lived in Switzerland during that time), or a stay in a Swiss institution.
A person who is affected by or threatened with unemployment must register with the RAV (regional employment center) for public job placement as early as possible, and at the latest on the first day for which they claim unemployment insurance benefits. Registration can be done online through the eService in Job-Room, or in person at the responsible RAV.
Within 15 days of registering for public job placement, the responsible RAV invites the claimant to an initial consultation. The claimant should bring their AHV card or health insurance card, an official ID (identity card, passport or foreign national's ID), proof of job search efforts, and, if they are an EU/EFTA citizen already drawing unemployment benefit from an EU/EFTA state while job-hunting in Switzerland, form PD U2.
Unemployment benefit generally amounts to 70 percent of the insured earnings, or 80 percent if the claimant has a maintenance obligation toward children under 25, if the insured earnings do not exceed CHF 3,797, or if the claimant receives an IV disability pension for a degree of disability of at least 40 percent. The maximum period for drawing benefit is 2 years (the framework period for benefit), which starts on the first day the claimant meets all the eligibility conditions.

Label: Compulsory accident insurance (UVG) and suspending accident cover in health insurance
Description: Explains who is compulsorily insured against occupational and non-occupational accidents under the accident insurance act (UVG), and how a person with full UVG accident cover can have the accident cover in their compulsory health insurance suspended. [FOPH]
Aliases: accident insurance; UVG accident cover; work accident insurance; leisure accident insurance; who is covered against accidents; Unfallversicherung; Berufsunfall; Nichtberufsunfall; suspend accident cover; Unfalldeckung sistieren; 8 hours a week accident insurance; domestic help accident insurance; Unfalldeckung ausschliessen; Bestaetigung des Arbeitgebers Unfallversicherung; Unfalldeckung bei der Krankenkasse; do I still need accident cover if I work; Berufsunfälle; Nichtberufsunfälle; Berufskrankheiten; UVG; Unfalldeckung; Sistierung; Heimarbeitende; Hausangestellte; Krankenversicherer; occupational accidents; non-occupational accidents; compulsory accident insurance; suspension of accident cover; household staff
Questions: Am I insured against accidents if I work fewer than 8 hours a week?; Can I suspend the accident cover in my health insurance because I am already insured through my employer?; Wer ist in der Schweiz obligatorisch gegen Unfälle versichert?
Published facts:
Every person employed in Switzerland is compulsorily insured under the accident insurance act (UVG) against occupational accidents and occupational illnesses; if they are employed for at least 8 hours per week with the same employer, they are also compulsorily insured against non-occupational accidents.
The compulsory accident insurance for employees also covers home workers, apprentices, interns, volunteers, persons working in training and disability workshops, domestic staff, and cleaners in private households.
Unemployed persons are, in principle, also compulsorily insured against accidents.
An insured person who has full accident-risk cover (occupational and non-occupational accidents) under the accident insurance act (UVG) can have their health insurer suspend the accident cover in their compulsory health insurance.
A person employed for at least 8 hours per week with an employer in Switzerland has full UVG accident-risk cover and can therefore have their health insurer suspend the accident cover.
The health insurer arranges the suspension of the accident cover when the insured person requests it and proves they are fully insured under the accident insurance act (UVG); the suspension begins at the earliest on the first day of the month following the request, and the health insurer reduces the premium accordingly.
A person who is not or no longer employed, or who works fewer than 8 hours per week, is not compulsorily insured under the accident insurance act (UVG) (for example children, homemakers, students and pensioners), and must insure themselves against accidents through the compulsory health insurance instead.

Label: Importing moving goods (household effects and vehicles) when moving to Switzerland
Description: Explains the conditions for the duty-free import of household goods, vehicles and other belongings when moving your residence to Switzerland, the form and documents to declare at the border, and the deadline. [BAZG, ch.ch]
Aliases: Moebel beim Zuzug; Hausrat am Zoll; duty-free moving goods; Übersiedlungsgut; import household goods Switzerland; moving goods customs form; bringing my car when I move to Switzerland; Zoll beim Umzug in die Schweiz; customs declaration moving to Switzerland; 6 months prior use rule; deadline duty-free import; second home vehicle customs; Handelswaren; Umzugsgut; abgabenfrei; Wohnsitzverlegung; Einreisezollstelle; Aufenthaltsbewilligung; Abmeldebestätigung; Zollstellen; household effects; Transfer of domicile; household goods; customs office of importation
Questions: Can I bring my car into Switzerland duty-free when I move here?; What form do I need to declare my moving goods at Swiss customs?; Muss ich beim Umzug in die Schweiz für mein Auto Zoll bezahlen?
Published facts:
Relocating your residence to Switzerland is the most important condition for importing your household goods, any collections, animals, or your car duty-free; the imported goods must also have been used personally by you for at least 6 months before the move and must continue to be used by you after the import.
Household goods, personal effects and school material of students can be imported duty-free even if the student does not relocate their residence to Switzerland.
Persons living abroad who want to take up residence in Switzerland may import most of their belongings duty-free; this also applies to a move to a secondary residence in Switzerland, but for vehicles and animals customs duties must still be paid.
At the border you present the completed application form 18.44 (Übersiedlungsgut) to the entry customs office; the assessment of your moving goods must take place during the opening hours of the customs offices that handle commercial goods.
People moving from an EU-27 state (as of 1 February 2020) or an EFTA state do not need to present a confirmation of a residence permit; they can prove the relocation of residence by other means, such as an employment contract, a rental contract, or a deregistration confirmation from the country of departure.
You must import your belongings duty-free within two years of the date of the move.
At the border crossing you must present a complete list of all goods being imported, the customs form for duty-free import of moving goods (in duplicate), an identity document (passport or ID card), a document proving deregistration with the authorities of your country of origin, a Swiss residence permit or other document proving the change of residence (for example an employment contract or a rental contract), a foreign vehicle registration document for any vehicle, and proof of the purchase or rental of the accommodation.
Someone moving from one foreign country to another whose removal goods pass through Switzerland must declare them for transit.
The arrival with removal goods does not have to be announced in advance; a person can report on entry, during office hours, at a customs office responsible for commercial goods.
Removal goods can in principle be cleared only from Monday to Friday during the opening hours of the customs offices responsible for commercial goods, and at certain large offices also on Saturday morning.
Goods for which the conditions for exemption are not met, for example an item not used abroad for six months before the change of residence, must be listed at the end of the inventory or on a separate list under the heading "goods to be cleared", with their value.
Where the required documents are not yet available, the customs office can carry out a provisional clearance at the request of the person carrying the goods and will ask for a security, which is paid back less a processing fee once the documents are supplied within six months.
Presenting a residence permit is not an absolute condition, for example for EU citizens; proof of the change of residence has to be brought instead, and deregistration in the country of origin together with an employment contract and a rental contract can serve as that proof.
Later consignments must be declared to the customs office on a separate list already at the first import, and this can also concern a passenger car or another private vehicle imported separately.
There are no eased import requirements for plants brought as removal goods from a country outside the EU, while for plants brought as removal goods from the EU there are, and in that case the plants need no plant passport.
Special rules apply to removal goods that contain ivory or parts made of ivory, such as a piano or ornaments, and to stuffed animals, and the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office in Bern gives the information needed.
Special rules apply to weapons in removal goods, and the Federal Office of Police in Bern gives the information needed.

Label: Family allowances (federal minimum)
Description: What Swiss family allowances are, the federal minimum monthly rates for the child and education allowance, who is entitled, the one-allowance-per-child rule, and that cantons may set higher amounts [BSV].
Aliases: family allowance; child allowance; education allowance; Familienzulage; Kinderzulage; Ausbildungszulage; birth allowance; adoption allowance; how much is family allowance Switzerland; who gets child allowance; Geburtszulage; Adoptionszulage; Anspruchskonkurrenz; Verbot des Doppelbezugs; Erwerbstätigkeitsprinzip
Questions: How much is the child allowance in Switzerland?; Wie viel Familienzulage bekomme ich pro Kind?; Can both parents get family allowance for the same child?
Published facts:
Family allowances are a form of social security and family policy meant to partly offset the costs of caring for one or more children; they comprise the child allowance, the education allowance, the birth allowance and the adoption allowance.
The federal Family Allowances Act (FamZG), in force since 1 January 2009, provides a degree of harmonization but leaves the cantons room to set the level of benefits, the organization and the financing of family allowances.
The child allowance is paid from the month of the child's birth until the end of the month in which the child turns 16; if the education allowance already applies before the 16th birthday, that allowance is paid instead. The federal minimum is CHF 215 per month, and cantons may set a higher rate.
The education allowance is paid from the start of the month the child begins post-compulsory education, at the earliest from the end of the month the child turns 15, until the education ends, and at the latest until the end of the month the child turns 25. The federal minimum is CHF 268 per month, and cantons may set a higher rate.
A birth allowance, paid for each child born alive or after at least 23 weeks of pregnancy, is optional for cantons to introduce and set the amount of; the cantons of Fribourg, Geneva, Jura, Lucerne, Neuchatel, Schwyz, Uri, Valais and Vaud pay one.
An adoption allowance is paid once for each minor child taken in for later adoption, but not for a step-child adoption under Article 264c of the Civil Code; it is optional for cantons to introduce and set the amount of, and is paid in the cantons of Fribourg, Geneva, Jura, Lucerne, Neuchatel, Uri, Valais and Vaud.
Employees and self-employed persons are entitled to family allowances if their AHV-liable income is at least CHF 630 per month or CHF 7,560 per year; below that threshold they count as non-employed. Non-employed persons with modest income are entitled if their taxable income does not exceed CHF 45,360 per year, they count as non-employed under AHV rules, they are resident in Switzerland, and they do not receive supplementary benefits to the AHV/IV.
Only one allowance of the same type may be paid per child (prohibition of double payment). If several people are entitled to allowances for the same child, payment follows this order: the employed person before the non-employed person; if both are employed, the parent with parental custody; then the parent the child mainly lives with; then the parent working in the child's canton of residence; and finally the parent with the higher AHV-liable income from employment, or from self-employment if neither parent has employment income.
Special conditions apply to the payment of family allowances for children who live abroad.

Label: Family allowances in the canton of Zurich
Description: The Zurich child and education allowance rates, who pays family allowances for employees and for non-employed persons, and the conditions and time limit for claiming them in the canton of Zurich [SVA Zurich].
Aliases: family allowance Zurich; Kinderzulage Zurich; Familienzulagen Zurich; child allowance amount Zurich; family allowance for non-employed Zurich; Zulage fuer Nichterwerbstaetige; who pays family allowance Zurich; wie hoch ist die Kinderzulage im Kanton Zuerich; AHV-Ausgleichskasse Familienzulagen; retroactive family allowance claim; Ausbildungszulagen; AHV-pflichtigen Einkommen; AHV-Ausgleichskasse; Referenzalter; Taggeld der Arbeitslosenversicherung; gesetzlichen Bestimmungen
Questions: How much is the child allowance in the canton of Zurich?; Wie beantrage ich Familienzulagen als Nichterwerbstaetige im Kanton Zuerich?; Who pays my family allowance if I am not employed?
Published facts:
Canton of Zurich: family allowances comprise a child allowance of CHF 215 per month up to the child's 12th birthday, then CHF 268 per month up to the 16th birthday, and an education allowance of CHF 268 per month from the 16th to the 25th birthday while in training. If training starts before the 16th birthday, the education allowance begins once the child is 15 years old and has finished compulsory schooling.
Canton of Zurich: employees claim family allowances through their employer. The employer's family compensation fund checks whether the conditions are met and, if so, informs the employer, who pays the allowance together with the wage.
Canton of Zurich: non-employed persons claim family allowances at the family compensation fund of their AHV compensation office; it checks whether the conditions are met and, if so, the AHV compensation office pays the allowance monthly.
Canton of Zurich: a non-employed person is entitled to family allowances only if their taxable income for direct federal tax is not higher than CHF 45,360, they are compulsorily insured and liable to contribute under the AHV, and they do not receive supplementary benefits.
Canton of Zurich: a non-employed person has no entitlement to family allowances if the other parent can claim them as an employee or self-employed person, if the other parent is entitled to unemployment daily allowances and thus also to family allowances, or if their spouse or registered partner has reached the AHV reference age.
Canton of Zurich: employees are entitled to family allowances if their AHV-liable income is at least CHF 7,560 per year or CHF 630 per month. If a person has several employers, the total earned income counts, and the company paying the highest wage is responsible for paying the allowance.
Canton of Zurich: family allowances can be claimed retroactively for at most 5 years; entitlement and payment are governed by the legal provisions in force at the relevant time.

Label: Maternity, other-parent and adoption leave
Description: Federal maternity leave and income compensation, the leave of the other parent, and adoption leave, including durations, percentages, daily maximum and who is entitled [BSV].
Aliases: maternity leave; Mutterschaftsurlaub; paternity leave; Vaterschaftsurlaub; adoption leave; Adoptionsurlaub; parental leave Switzerland; how many weeks maternity leave; father leave after birth; maternity pay percentage; Erwerbsersatzentschädigung; Mutterschaftsentschädigung; Samenspende; EO-Beiträge; Entschädigung des andern Elternteils; Adoptionsentschädigung
Questions: How long is maternity leave in Switzerland?; Wie viele Wochen Vaterschaftsurlaub gibt es?; Do I get paid leave if I adopt a child?
Published facts:
A person who is employed or self-employed is entitled to income compensation (EO) after the birth or adoption of a child if they have paid EO contributions for at least 9 months before the birth or adoption and were gainfully employed for at least 5 of those months; for an adoption, the child must be younger than 4 years old.
Employed mothers are entitled to a maternity leave of 14 weeks, which must be taken immediately after the birth and in one block. The maternity allowance is paid as a daily allowance of 80 percent of the average earned income before the birth, up to a maximum of CHF 220 per day; the maximum is reached at a monthly income of CHF 8,250 for employees, or a yearly income of CHF 99,000 for self-employed women.
If a newborn must stay in hospital for more than 2 weeks directly after the birth, the mother is entitled to up to 8 additional weeks of maternity allowance, provided she continues working after the regular maternity leave; this extension is paid through the income compensation scheme.
If the mother dies shortly after the birth, the surviving father, or the mother's wife if she meets the conditions for other-parent leave, is entitled to 14 weeks of leave taken in one block starting the day after the mother's death. If the father dies shortly after the birth, the surviving mother is entitled to 2 additional weeks of leave on top of the 14-week maternity leave, which can be taken flexibly like the other-parent leave.
The other parent (the father, or the mother's wife where she qualifies) is entitled to 2 weeks of paid leave, to be taken within 6 months of the birth, either in one block including weekends or day by day. The allowance is 80 percent of the average earned income before the birth, up to CHF 220 per day; 14 daily allowances are paid for the 2 weeks, giving a maximum of CHF 3,080.
The recipient of the other-parent allowance must be the child's legal father, or the mother's wife if she was married to the mother at the time of the birth and the child was conceived through sperm donation under the law on medically assisted reproduction. There is no entitlement to the other-parent allowance for an adoption; only the adoption allowance applies in that case.
Employees who take in a child under 4 years old for adoption are entitled to 2 weeks of paid adoption leave, to be taken within the first year after the adoption, either in one block including weekends or day by day (10 days). The adoptive parents choose which of them takes the leave and may split it between them but cannot take it at the same time; no compensated leave is provided for adopting a partner's child (step-child adoption).
The adoption allowance is 80 percent of the average earned income before the adoption, up to a maximum of CHF 220 per day; 14 daily allowances are paid for the 2 weeks of leave, giving a maximum of CHF 3,080.

Label: Tenancy agreement: contents, deposit, subletting and termination
Description: Explains what a residential lease in Switzerland should contain, the rules for the rent deposit and subletting, and how notice and termination of a lease work, including the conciliation authority for disputes. [ch.ch, Fedlex]
Aliases: rental deposit; Mietkaution; how much deposit can landlord ask; subletting my apartment; Untermiete erlaubt; notice period apartment Switzerland; Kündigungsfrist Wohnung; terminate a lease in Switzerland; spouse consent to terminate lease; what should be in a tenancy agreement; notice period for a flat; moving out before the notice date; Nachmieter; Wohnung kündigen; maximale Mietkaution; Mietzinsdepot; Kaution; Kündigungsfristen; Untermiete; Wohngemeinschaften; Mietsache; Nebenkosten; Ehepartnerin; Härtefall; Schlichtungsbehörde; eingetragenen Partnerschaften
Questions: What should a Swiss tenancy agreement include?; Wie viel Kaution darf der Vermieter für eine Wohnung verlangen?; Can I sublet my apartment without the landlord's permission?
Published facts:
A lease usually names the tenant party in writing (for a family home it is useful to also name the spouse; in a shared flat or concubinage all persons named in the lease are jointly and severally liable for the rent), describes the rented object (usually a flat, including rooms such as attic and cellar and shared use of areas like the laundry), and states whether the lease runs for a fixed term or an indefinite period, most leases being indefinite. It should also state the notice periods and termination dates and the monthly rent and ancillary costs; if the lease does not itemize the ancillary costs, they are considered included in the rent.
A tenant of a home or business premises pays a rent deposit (Mietzinsdepot, also called Kaution) only if the lease requires it; for homes the deposit is at most three months' rent. If the tenant provides the security in cash or securities, the landlord must deposit it at a bank in a savings account or deposit account in the tenant's name.
A tenant may sublet the whole flat or a single room, but must inform the landlord about it.
The landlord may refuse subletting only if the tenant refuses to disclose the details of the subletting, if the tenant charges an excessive rent for it (for a furnished flat a surcharge of at most 20 percent may be charged for wear of the furnishings; otherwise the tenant should charge no more than they themselves pay, including ancillary costs), or if the subletting causes the landlord a substantial disadvantage.
For the rental of flats, the parties may give notice with three months' notice for a date customary at the place, or, if there is no local custom, for the end of a three-month rental period.
Landlord and tenant of a home or business premises must give notice in writing. The landlord must use a form approved by the canton that states how the tenant must proceed if they want to challenge the notice or request an extension of the tenancy.
If several persons signed the lease, all of them must sign a notice of termination. In a family or a registered partnership, a tenant can give notice only with the consent of the other spouse or partner, even if only one of them signed the lease; a tenant does not have to state a reason for their own notice and should send it by registered letter to the landlord.
A tenant who returns the rented object without observing the notice period or termination date is released from their obligations toward the landlord only if they propose a new tenant who is acceptable to the landlord, solvent, and willing to take over the lease on the same terms; otherwise the tenant must keep paying the rent until the tenancy ends according to the contract or the law.
A tenant has the right to learn the landlord's reason for a notice of termination, and can challenge the notice within 30 days at the conciliation authority of their municipality if it is abusive, for example because the tenant asked for a rent reduction or the correction of a defect, or because the tenant's family circumstances changed. If the notice is valid, the tenant is nonetheless entitled to an extension of the tenancy in cases of hardship, for example tight financial circumstances, illness, or the situation on the rental housing market.

Label: Rent increases, the reference interest rate and defects
Description: Explains when and how a landlord may raise the rent, how the mortgage reference interest rate affects rent increases and reductions, how a tenant can challenge the initial rent, and how to report defects in a rented home. [ch.ch, BWO, Fedlex]
Aliases: rent increase Switzerland; Mietzinserhöhung; reference interest rate; Referenzzinssatz; how to request a rent reduction; Mietzinssenkung verlangen; challenge the initial rent; Anfangsmietzins anfechten; report a defect in my flat; Mängelliste beim Einzug; defect in the flat; Mangel in der Wohnung; Mieterhöhung; Kündigungsfrist; Mängelliste; Wohnungsübergabeprotokoll; Mängelrüge; Vormieterschaft; Anfangsmietzins; Mietzinssenkung; Prozentpunkte; Kühlschrank; Mängelrüge; Renovationen
Questions: How much can my landlord raise my rent when the reference interest rate goes up?; Wie fordere ich eine Mietzinssenkung, wenn der Referenzzinssatz sinkt?; Can I challenge the rent I was charged when I moved in?
Published facts:
A landlord may generally increase the rent if general prices rise (inflation), if the mortgage reference interest rate has been raised, if maintenance and operating costs have increased (for example administrative costs or property taxes), or if major conversions or renovations with improvements have been carried out.
The landlord must notify a rent increase to the tenant on an official form and give reasons for it; the increase must reach the tenant at least 10 days before the start of the ordinary notice period, and the landlord can raise the rent only for the next possible termination date.
The mortgage reference interest rate (Referenzzinssatz) that governs rent adjustments is 1.25 percent, valid since 2 September 2025; the Federal Office for Housing's page, saved on 18 September 2026, states that it remains unchanged from 2 September 2026.
If the mortgage reference interest rate rises by 0.25 percentage points, the rent can be increased by 3 percent; if it falls by 0.25 percentage points, tenants are in principle entitled to a rent reduction of 2.91 percent for that step.
To request a rent reduction, a tenant should send a request to the landlord, ideally by registered letter; the landlord must respond within 30 days and may accept the request and lower the rent, or reject it, or offset it against other cost factors while explaining why. If the tenant disagrees with the answer, or receives no answer within 30 days, they can turn to the conciliation authority, but must do so within 30 days of that deadline, meaning at the latest 60 days after the original request to the landlord.
A tenant can challenge the initial rent as abusive within 30 days of taking over the rented object, if they were forced into the contract by personal or family hardship or by the situation on the local housing market, or if the landlord raised the initial rent significantly compared to the previous tenant's rent, for example if the new rent is at least 10 percent higher than what the previous tenant paid.
Tenancy law distinguishes a severe defect (the home is practically uninhabitable, for example after a burst water pipe), a medium defect (the home remains habitable but its usability is reduced, for example a broken refrigerator), and a small defect (such as blown fuses, burnt-out light bulbs, or worn seals); tenants must generally repair and pay for small defects themselves.
At the start of the tenancy, a tenant should insist that a deficiency list (Mängelliste) is drawn up, ideally as part of the handover record. For medium and severe defects arising during the tenancy, the tenant should report the defect promptly and, if nothing happens, send the landlord a registered letter describing and photographing the defect and setting a reasonable deadline, for example 14 days, to fix it.

Label: Canton of Zurich: initial rent notification form
Description: Explains the Canton of Zurich's duty to notify the initial rent on an official form when a new residential lease is concluded, and which official tenancy forms the canton provides. [Canton of Zurich]

Questions: Does my landlord have to notify the starting rent on an official form in Zurich?; Welches Formular brauche ich für die Mitteilung des Anfangsmietzinses im Kanton Zürich?; Where can I download the official Zurich tenancy forms?
Published facts:
Canton of Zurich: since 1 November 2013, when a new lease for a home is concluded, the landlord must use the form for notifying the initial rent under Article 270 paragraph 2 of the Code of Obligations (Section 229b of the cantonal Introductory Act to the Swiss Civil Code); for this notification the landlord must use either the official form issued by the Canton of Zurich or their own form approved by the Directorate of Justice and Home Affairs.
Canton of Zurich: these official forms can be downloaded electronically or ordered in paper form from the cantonal printed-matter and materials center (KDMZ); paper forms get a new print date at each print run but their content does not change, so forms with an older date remain valid.
Canton of Zurich: the Directorate of Justice and Home Affairs is responsible only for providing and approving these tenancy forms; for legal advice on tenancy and lease law, tenants and landlords must contact the district court or conciliation authority of their district.
Canton of Zurich: a landlord who does not want to use the official forms may use their own form, but it must be approved by the Directorate of Justice and Home Affairs before use, and it must carry an approval note naming the Directorate and the date of approval.

Label: Getting married in Switzerland
Description: Federal overview of who may marry in Switzerland, the marriage preparation procedure, the waiting time before and cost of the civil wedding, marriage for all, and what to report afterward. [ch.ch]
Aliases: getting married in Switzerland; marriage preparation procedure; heiraten in der Schweiz; Ehevorbereitungsverfahren; civil wedding cost Switzerland; entry visa for marriage; marriage for all Switzerland; witnesses required at wedding; does marrying a Swiss citizen give citizenship; Einreisevisum; Zivilstandsamt; Trauzeuginnen; urteilsfähig; eingetragene Partnerschaften; vereinfachtes Einbürgerungsverfahren; Schweizer Bürgerrecht; zivile Trauung; kantonalen Steuerverwaltung
Questions: What documents and visa do I need to get married in Switzerland as a foreign national?; How much does a civil wedding cost in Switzerland?; Wie lange dauert das Ehevorbereitungsverfahren und wie viel Zeit habe ich danach, um zu heiraten?
Published facts:
To marry in Switzerland, both future spouses must be at least 18 years old, have the capacity of judgement, not already be married or in a registered partnership, and not be related to each other in a direct line or as siblings.
A person without Swiss citizenship may need an entry visa for the wedding in Switzerland depending on their country of origin; the civil registry office or the Swiss representation abroad informs the couple which documents to submit, and after the check both partners fill in and sign the form 'Erklärung betreffend die Voraussetzungen für die Eheschliessung' there.
Once the civil registry office confirms that all formalities for the marriage are complete, the couple has three months to hold the wedding.
The wedding may take place at the civil registry office of the couple's place of residence or, if they prefer, at another civil registry office in Switzerland; two witnesses who are of legal age and have the capacity of judgement must be present.
The cost of a civil wedding (documents and the marriage act) is between 300 and 400 Swiss francs nationwide; special requests, such as a wedding on a Saturday, incur additional costs.
Same-sex marriage has been possible in Switzerland since 1 July 2022; no new registered partnerships can be established, but an existing registered partnership can be converted into a marriage.
Marrying a Swiss citizen does not automatically grant Swiss citizenship, but the foreign spouse can go through a simplified naturalisation procedure.
After the wedding, the new marital status and any change of name must be reported to the municipal administration, the cantonal tax administration, the employer, the bank, the post office, and insurers.
